title: Why Do Great Flood Myths Seem To Be Universal?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore why flood myths appear across many cultures. They begin with the Noah's flood story and George Smith's 1872 discovery of the Epic of Gilgamesh flood tablet, then cover 18th–19th century deluvialism and why geology rejects a global flood. They lay out explanations for universal flood myths: a localized flood spread by migrating groups (Proto Indo Europeans), common riverine flooding, and Christian missionary influence (South Pacific Maori). They introduce geomythology, examples of flood legends with geological backing (Emperor Yu China, Black Sea/Bosporus flood, Persian Gulf, Doggerland and the Storegga slide, Pacific Northwest tsunami legends, Zuni marine fossils), recurring mythic themes (survivor couple, divine punishment, purification, return to primordial ocean, human industriousness), and dismissed psychoanalytic theories. Ends with a listener mail about the Stuff You Should Know 5K.

segments.title: Live show promo (San Francisco SketchFest)
segments.summary: Hosts promote a live Stuff You Should Know show at SF Sketchfest in San Francisco on January 1 and note the vaccination requirement.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to Noah's flood
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about Chuck's cold and Jerry the rear admiral, then introduce the Noah's flood story as the starting point for the discussion of a possible historical flood.

segments.title: George Smith and the Epic of Gilgamesh flood story
segments.summary: George Smith, an amateur Assyriologist, read a flood story in cuneiform in the Epic of Gilgamesh in 1872 that resembles the Noah account. Differences include the gods angered by noisy humans, the flood hero Utnapishtim, and birds sent out to find land. The hosts note the epic predates the Old Testament.

segments.title: Deluvialism and the geological record
segments.summary: The hosts describe 18th and 19th century deluvialism, which held that a biblical flood shaped the Earth's geology, and explain that the geological record later contradicted it, showing slow layer-by-layer formation. They raise why flood myths seem universal.

segments.title: Explanations for universal flood myths
segments.summary: A study of about fifty cultures found flood myths tied to punishment. Explanations include a localized flood spread by migrating groups such as the Proto Indo Europeans, which would explain the absence of flood myths in Sub-Saharan Africa; frequent local floods; and Christian missionaries spreading the Noah story, as seen in the South Pacific Maori myths that shifted from tsunami-based to deluge-based after 1814 contact.

segments.title: Mid-episode break
segments.summary: Brief break in which Chuck blows his nose, followed by banter about sneezing on stage and Barry Manilow.

segments.title: Introduction to geomythology
segments.summary: The hosts define geomythology as a field, mostly led by trained geologists, that reads myths as containing eyewitness accounts of natural disasters, with the events cloaked in mythic language. Volcano legends and nuclear waste warning myths are used as examples of pre-scientific warning systems.

segments.title: Geomythology case studies: Emperor Yu, Black Sea flood, Persian Gulf, Doggerland
segments.summary: Examples include a 2016 study linking Chinese Emperor Yu's flood myth to a landslide-dammed lake that burst within a year, the Ryan and Pitman hypothesis of a Mediterranean breach at the Bosporus about 7,000 years ago, the proposed submerged Persian Gulf settlements, and Doggerland with the Storegga slide tsunami about 8,500 years ago and a Breton flood legend.

segments.title: Pacific Northwest tsunami legend and Zuni fossils
segments.summary: Hoh and Quileute legends of a thunderbird and whale fight are matched to a magnitude nine earthquake and tsunami around 1700 that reached Japan, noted in a Japanese temple record. The Zuni creation story explains marine fossils found in the desert.

segments.title: Recurring themes in flood myths
segments.summary: Common elements include a surviving man and wife who repopulate the Earth, divine warnings, purposes such as apocalypse, purification, and return to a primordial ocean, and stories of human industriousness such as Emperor Yu, the Bhutan lake-draining legend, and an Aboriginal boulder-rolling story. The Chinese brother-and-sister legend is discussed.
topics: Chinese brother and sister flood myth

segments.title: Psychoanalytic explanations dismissed
segments.summary: The hosts mention a 1930s Hungarian psychoanalyst who attributed flood myths to dreams caused by nighttime urination and other psychoanalytic theories, and they dismiss these in favor of geomythology.

segments.title: Listener mail: Stuff You Should Know 5K
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the virtual Stuff You Should Know 5K run and congratulate Amanda Thompson, the fastest woman finisher, who received a hand-crafted metal rack. They ask listeners to remind them about the next event in late summer or fall.
